entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Zhang Ji (died 196 CE) was a prominent military general who served the formidable warlord Dong Zhuo during the turbulent twilight years of the Eastern Han dynasty in ancient China. His actions, particularly his role in the post-assassination power struggles and the subsequent seizure of the imperial capital Chang'an, were instrumental in prolonging the period of imperial collapse and accelerating the fragmentation of central authority that defined the pre-Three Kingdoms era. Operating within a volatile political landscape characterized by opportunistic warlordism and widespread rebellion, Zhang Ji's career exemplifies the brutal realities of power consolidation and territorial control during one of China's most chaotic periods.

Following Dong Zhuo's assassination in 192 CE by Lü Bu and Wang Yun, Zhang Ji, alongside fellow generals Li Jue, Guo Si, and Fan Chou, initially sought amnesty from the new Han court. Upon being refused, they rallied their forces, numbering in the tens of thousands, and launched a devastating assault on Chang'an. In June 192 CE, their combined forces overwhelmed the city's defenses, killed Wang Yun, and effectively seized control of the child Emperor Xian, thereby re-establishing a corrupt and puppet regime that further eroded the Han dynasty's legitimacy. Zhang Ji was subsequently granted the title General Who Guards the East (鎮東將軍) and enfeoffed as Marquis of Pingyang, wielding considerable influence within the new power structure that controlled the emperor for the next four years.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Zhang Ji's actions, particularly his role in the 192 CE Chang'an coup, directly prolonged the collapse of the Eastern Han dynasty and set the stage for the Three Kingdoms period by maintaining a puppet imperial court. His death led to his nephew Zhang Xiu's rise, who later inflicted a major defeat on Cao Cao, thus having a tangible impact on the regional power dynamics of late 2nd century China.
